channel.title: OSA Paper Podcast
channel.description:
Each weekday, one new paper on obstructive sleep apnea surgery: hypoglossal nerve stimulation, palate surgery including barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, tongue base, skeletal and nasal procedures, patient selection and comparators. Every episode summarizes the paper, walks through it as a teaching round, places it against a 440-paper evidence library, and ends with whether it should change practice.
Episodes are written and narrated by an AI system working from the full text of each paper and the host's curated library of digests, under rules set by the host. They are reviewed for teaching, not for patient care. Nothing here is medical advice.
Produced by Ryan Nord, MD (VCU Health). Disclosures: consultant to AvivoMed; previously a consultant to Inspire Medical Systems (ended 2025) and Medtronic. No company funds or reviews this podcast.

item.title: Oropharyngeal Lateral Wall Collapse on Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy as a Predictor of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Response in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea-A Systematic Review
item.itunes:title: Oropharyngeal Lateral Wall Collapse on Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy as a Predictor of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Response in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea-A Systematic Review
item.description:
So, what does this systematic review mean for our clinical practice?
In terms of an explicit call: watch. There is no change to our implant candidacy gate, but we must maintain a close watch on emerging trials of concurrent pharyngeal reconstruction.
Let us break down the exact decisions affected in clinic and the operating room.
First, candidate counseling. When I perform drug-induced sleep endoscopy on an Inspire candidate and observe complete oropharyngeal lateral wall collapse, I do not deny them surgery. Complete concentric collapse at the soft palate remains our only absolute anatomical exclusion. However, I change the conversation.
I tell the patient directly: if your lateral walls remained open, your expected chance of surgical success would be roughly seventy-five to eighty-five percent. With complete side-wall collapse, your expected chance of success drops by about fifteen to twenty percentage points, down to roughly fifty-eight to sixty-seven percent. But two out of three patients with this pattern still achieve success, your nightly device usage is expected to be just as high, and your stimulation voltage requirements are identical.
Second, risk stratification by body mass index. When I see complete lateral wall collapse, I look immediately at the patient's body mass index. If their body mass index is twenty-eight or twenty-nine, I am very comfortable proceeding; data from Vena and Huyett show their response rate will likely stay near seventy percent. If their body mass index is thirty-two or thirty-three, or pushing into the newly expanded thirty-five to forty range, I have a much more sobering discussion. I explain that adiposity and lateral wall collapse act synergistically to cut response rates in half, and I make weight loss and lifestyle modification an active, mandatory part of our preoperative and postoperative plan.
Third, our surgical technique. Classic U-triple-P is historical context; that is not what we do. In our practice, when we need to reconstruct the pharynx, we perform barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, or B-R-P. As you have seen me do in the operating room, B-R-P suspends and repositions the lateral pharyngeal walls anteriorly and laterally to the pterygomandibular raphe using knotless barbed sutures.

I explain that adiposity and lateral wall collapse act synergistically to cut response rates in half, and I make weight loss and lifestyle modification an active, mandatory part of our preoperative and postoperative plan.

Third, our surgical technique. Classic U-triple-P is historical context; that is not what we do. In our practice, when we need to reconstruct the pharynx, we perform barbed reposition pharyngoplasty, or B-R-P. As you have seen me do in the operating room, B-R-P suspends and repositions the lateral pharyngeal walls anteriorly and laterally to the pterygomandibular raphe using knotless barbed sutures.

When you see Huyett's combination tonsillectomy data showing an eighty-five percent A-H-I reduction but a six point seven percent return to the operating room for hemorrhage, that should give you pause. Traditional cold or electrocautery tonsillectomy leaves a raw, open granulating muscle bed in an adult sleep apnea patient. If we decide to address the lateral walls surgically alongside neurostimulation, B-R-P allows us to stabilize the lateral muscular sleeve and re-approximate mucosal pillars, which provides structural lateral wall tension while mitigating the catastrophic bleeding risks of exposed muscular beds. We do not routine-order concurrent tonsillectomy on every lateral wall patient today, but in patients with prominent tonsils and complete lateral collapse, concurrent B-R-P is the technique we are watching and evaluating.

Fourth, perioperative orders. Remember our owner ruling: patients admitted for a twenty-three-hour observation stay must always be managed and documented as a twenty-three-hour observation stay. Never refer to these patients as outpatient. If we perform an Inspire implant combined with pharyngeal surgery like B-R-P in a complete lateral wall patient, they are at higher risk for airway swelling and pain. They stay on our twenty-three-hour observation pathway, receive scheduled multimodal non-opioid analgesia, and are monitored closely overnight.

Fifth, postoperative management. When these patients return at three months, remember that a titration sleep study will paint an overly optimistic picture. If a complete lateral wall patient has a borderline titration study or reports lingering daytime fatigue, we do not declare victory; we order an entire-night home sleep apnea test. And as our twenty-twenty-four data demonstrated, we maintain a very low threshold for early awake flexible endoscopy in the clinic to visualize the palate and tongue base under active stimulation and optimize our electrode programming.

Our confidence in this approach is high, supported by low-certainty GRADE prognostic evidence that clearly refutes an absolute exclusion. What evidence would move my practice to a formal change? A randomized controlled trial comparing Inspire alone versus Inspire plus barbed reposition pharyngoplasty in patients with complete lateral wall collapse, measuring entire-night efficacy and long-term durability. Until such a trial is conducted, we counsel with nuance, we stratify by body mass index, and we offer therapy to candidates who still have a two-in-three chance of success.

The formal citation for this paper is: McBrinn S, Skan O, Iacovidou A. Oropharyngeal Lateral Wall Collapse on Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy as a Predictor of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Response in Obstructive Sleep Apnea, A Systematic Review. Diagnostics twenty-twenty-six, volume sixteen, issue sixteen, article twenty-five twenty-nine.

Before we walk into morning clinic, let me leave you with this question: when you see complete lateral wall collapse on sleep endoscopy in a patient with a body mass index of thirty-two, what is your threshold for offering hypoglossal nerve stimulation alone versus recommending concurrent palate or lateral wall surgery?

Think about that, and I will see you in the OR or clinic.

Paper: McBrinn S, Skan O, Iacovidou A. "Oropharyngeal Lateral Wall Collapse on Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy as a Predictor of Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation Response in Obstructive Sleep Apnoea—A Systematic Review." *Diagnostics* 2026;16:2529 (20 pages; issue number not printed). DOI: 10.3390/diagnostics16162529 (printed). PMID: not printed in PDF (42650932 per PubMed via the weekly scan). Received 18 June 2026; revised 9 July 2026; accepted 10 July 2026; published 11 August 2026. Imperial College NHS Foundation Trust and Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, London. Open access (CC BY). https://doi.org/10.3390/diagnostics16162529

item.title: Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP)
item.itunes:title: Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty (BSBP)
item.description:
My practice call for this paper is watch.
This paper does not change my primary surgical technique today, but it provides a compelling concept that I will watch closely as comparative data emerges.
Here is why. In my practice, barbed reposition pharyngoplasty is the primary palate procedure I perform. It is a fantastic tool, especially for patients with significant lateral pharyngeal wall collapse or complete concentric collapse at the velum. But the classic technique, which involves dissecting the supratonsillar fat pad and transecting the lower palatopharyngeus, is reproducible and provides robust lateral anchoring. While the idea of sparing the muscle bundle and creating a cable-stayed suspension is physiologically appealing, an uncontrolled thirty-patient series without long-term follow-up or post-operative sleep endoscopy is not enough evidence to abandon an established, proven technique.
However, this paper does directly influence several aspects of patient care in my clinic.
First, it sharpens my patient counseling. When I talk to patients preparing for a barbed pharyngoplasty, I can now give them very specific recovery timelines grounded in prospectively validated scales. I tell them that their palatal swelling and pain will peak in the first twelve to twenty-four hours, but should improve dramatically by forty-eight hours. Most importantly, I counsel every patient that there is roughly a ten to sixteen percent chance that a small tip of the barbed suture will poke through the mucosal surface around two to four weeks postoperatively. I explain in advance that if they feel a scratchy sensation or foreign body when swallowing, it is not an infection or a surgical failure; it is simply a suture barb that we can trim painlessly with scissors at their postoperative visit in under thirty seconds.
Second, it reinforces my perioperative medical management. The dramatic clearance of edema and low pain scores in this Italian cohort highlight the potent anti-inflammatory benefit of short-course systemic corticosteroids. In my outpatient practice, where patients go home the same day rather than staying forty-eight hours in a hospital bed, providing a short perioperative steroid taper alongside scheduled non-opioid analgesics helps blunt that initial twelve-to-twenty-four-hour inflammatory peak and keeps rescue opioid use to a minimum.
Third, regarding surgical candidacy and device selection: this paper reinforces the phenotypic sweet spot for pharyngoplasty versus hypoglossal nerve stimulation. In a patient with a body mass index of twenty-six and isolated lateral oropharyngeal collapse, barbed pharyngoplasty is an outstanding single-stage solution. Conversely, if a patient is being evaluated for Inspire, remember that severe lateral wall collapse halves the odds of response to neurostimulation. In patients who present with multi-level or concentric velar collapse, techniques like B-R-P or this stayed-bridge modification serve an essential role, either as definitive treatment or as a preliminary stage to stabilize the lateral walls before placing a nerve stimulator.
What evidence would move my confidence to actually change my surgical dissection? I would need to see a prospective, randomized controlled trial comparing classic B-R-P against this stayed bridge technique, using identical perioperative analgesic and steroid regimens, with blinded scoring of postoperative pain, objective swallowing testing, and polysomnography out to at least one year. Until then, classic B-R-P remains my standard of care.
The citation for today's paper is Pace, Iannella, Maniaci, and colleagues, "Edema and Subjective Discomfort After Barbed Stayed Bridge Pharyngoplasty," published in the Journal of Clinical Medicine, volume fourteen, twenty-twenty

item.title: Consensus Statements Among European Sleep Surgery Experts on Tongue, Hypopharynx, and Supraglottis Associated With Snoring and Obstructive Sleep Apnea - Part 1 - Evaluation and Decision Making
item.itunes:title: Consensus Statements Among European Sleep Surgery Experts on Tongue, Hypopharynx, and Supraglottis Associated With Snoring and Obstructive Sleep Apnea - Part 1 - Evaluation and Decision Making
item.description:
What is the bottom line for my clinical practice? My explicit call on this paper is watch, accompanied by immediate operational reinforcement of our existing surgical protocols.
This paper does not require an immediate change in operative technique because it represents expert consensus on diagnostic workup and decision-making rather than a comparative trial. However, it provides robust peer-reviewed support for four clinical decisions in our practice.
First, regarding Inspire hypoglossal nerve stimulation candidacy: this consensus strongly supports our staging algorithm. When an adult presents with severe tongue base collapse on sleep endoscopy but also carries grade three or four palatine tonsils, statement twenty-one provides unanimous consensus backing to perform tonsillectomy and palate expansion first. We do not implant a neurostimulator through obstructing palatine tonsils. During pre-implant sleep endoscopy, we must also evaluate the supraglottic phenotypes detailed here. If you identify primary trapdoor or floppy epiglottic collapse folding over the laryngeal inlet, unilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulation alone may fail to recruit the epiglottis if the lingual surface is not directly tethered to the advancing tongue base. Identifying that phenotype preoperatively allows you to counsel the patient on potential concurrent or staged epiglottopexy.
Second, regarding barbed reposition pharyngoplasty: this paper reinforces our sequencing principles. Ryan performs barbed reposition pharyngoplasty as his primary palatal procedure, providing anterolateral suspension of the lateral pharyngeal walls without tissue excision. Statement seventeen establishes unanimous agreement that when lower airway collapse is suspected to be secondary to upstream flow limitation, the palate and lateral walls should be treated first. Stabilizing the velum with barbed reposition pharyngoplasty frequently relieves downstream negative suction pressures, converting what appeared to be severe hypopharyngeal collapse into a stable airway.
Third, regarding perioperative care: statement nine in the history section highlights that a history of nocturnal choking, stridor, or continuous positive airway pressure intolerance specifically driven by choking sensations reached eighty-three to ninety-two percent consensus as an indicator of supraglottic obstruction. When a patient reports that history, we treat them as high risk for dynamic laryngeal collapse, communicating directly with anesthesia for post-extubation precautions and maintaining continuous overnight oximetry.
Fourth, regarding surgical failure and follow-up: when a patient presents with persistent moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea after prior pharyngoplasty, statement five of the sleep endoscopy section gives us unanimous consensus backing to mandate a repeat drug-induced sleep endoscopy before offering secondary surgery. We do not guess at the failure mechanism from the clinic chair. A repeat sleep endoscopy is required to differentiate residual lateral wall collapse from persistent tongue base collapse, determining whether the patient needs hypoglossal nerve stimulation or skeletal surgery.
What evidence would move this call from watch to a definitive change in practice? We would need prospective cohort studies or clinical trials evaluating outcomes of staged versus synchronous palate and tongue surgery, along with validated reliability data demonstrating that classifying epiglottic collapse into trapdoor, floppy, or omega phenotypes improves surgical cure rates.
For your reference, the complete citation is: Olszewska, De Vito, Baptista, Delakorda, Heiser, Cheong, Plaza, Vanderveken, Perez-Martin, Kotecha, Maurer, and Vicini. Consensus Statements Among European Sleep Surgery Expert

We do not implant a neurostimulator through obstructing palatine tonsils. During pre-implant sleep endoscopy, we must also evaluate the supraglottic phenotypes detailed here. If you identify primary trapdoor or floppy epiglottic collapse folding over the laryngeal inlet, unilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulation alone may fail to recruit the epiglottis if the lingual surface is not directly tethered to the advancing tongue base. Identifying that phenotype preoperatively allows you to counsel the patient on potential concurrent or staged epiglottopexy.
Second, regarding barbed reposition pharyngoplasty: this paper reinforces our sequencing principles. Ryan performs barbed reposition pharyngoplasty as his primary palatal procedure, providing anterolateral suspension of the lateral pharyngeal walls without tissue excision. Statement seventeen establishes unanimous agreement that when lower airway collapse is suspected to be secondary to upstream flow limitation, the palate and lateral walls should be treated first. Stabilizing the velum with barbed reposition pharyngoplasty frequently relieves downstream negative suction pressures, converting what appeared to be severe hypopharyngeal collapse into a stable airway.
Third, regarding perioperative care: statement nine in the history section highlights that a history of nocturnal choking, stridor, or continuous positive airway pressure intolerance specifically driven by choking sensations reached eighty-three to ninety-two percent consensus as an indicator of supraglottic obstruction. When a patient reports that history, we treat them as high risk for dynamic laryngeal collapse, communicating directly with anesthesia for post-extubation precautions and maintaining continuous overnight oximetry.
Fourth, regarding surgical failure and follow-up: when a patient presents with persistent moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea after prior pharyngoplasty, statement five of the sleep endoscopy section gives us unanimous consensus backing to mandate a repeat drug-induced sleep endoscopy before offering secondary surgery. We do not guess at the failure mechanism from the clinic chair. A repeat sleep endoscopy is required to differentiate residual lateral wall collapse from persistent tongue base collapse, determining whether the patient needs hypoglossal nerve stimulation or skeletal surgery.
What evidence would move this call from watch to a definitive change in practice? We would need prospective cohort studies or clinical trials evaluating outcomes of staged versus synchronous palate and tongue surgery, along with validated reliability data demonstrating that classifying epiglottic collapse into trapdoor, floppy, or omega phenotypes improves surgical cure rates.
For your reference, the complete citation is: Olszewska, De Vito, Baptista, Delakorda, Heiser, Cheong, Plaza, Vanderveken, Perez-Martin, Kotecha, Maurer, and Vicini. Consensus Statements Among European Sleep Surgery Expert
